scores.values_concern: Handover should start by asking what the carer is willing and able to do; do not assume the carer will absorb new nursing tasks by default.
scores.accuracy_concern: The 25% and 24% are relative reductions pooled across varied multicomponent discharge programmes; the meta-analysis cannot isolate the carer component, absolute readmission rates are needed for an N in 100 statement, and any shorter-term (30-day) result should be checked and stated if it was not clear.
scores.sharpen: Lead with absolute readmission figures from the full text and make 'What are you willing and able to do?' the first item on the handover checklist.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Care Act section 10 duty rests on the appearance of need in England; Scotland's adult carer support plan duty is worded differently and Wales and Northern Ireland differ; the census statistic on older carers' hours is unverified and should be dropped unless checked.
scores.sharpen: Drop the census figure unless verified, and state the English and Scottish entitlements in one plain sentence each on the card.

scores.accuracy_concern: Losing paid work on a client's death comes from the New York study; say it about England only if Skills for Care data on zero-hours contracts is verified, and draw the list of supports only from the English study.
scores.sharpen: Add one line for families (tell the care worker yourself, and invite them to the funeral if you wish) so the post gives relatives an action as well as agencies.

scores.accuracy_concern: The two trials differ in population (UK mixed carers versus US spouse carers), intervention and era, so the side-by-side card must not imply one programme is better; care home admission was a secondary outcome in START; a 2-point HADS difference needs a plain reading.
scores.sharpen: Open with the question of what should count as success, and state the size of START's effect on carers in plain words rather than as a HADS score.

scores.accuracy_concern: The claim that providers and commissioners do not usually report the number of distinct care workers is unsourced; the NICE NG21 continuity recommendation has to be quoted from the document; the illustrative calendar must stay clearly labelled as not real data.
scores.sharpen: Soften or drop the 'not usually reported' claim and anchor the post on the NICE NG21 recommendation plus one study of what home care users say about seeing the same workers.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Schulz 2003 carers were in the final year of the person's life with advanced dementia, so the figures do not describe dementia carers in general; 46 hours was the median for help with daily activities, not total time.
scores.sharpen: Open with the assessment question ('How long can you leave him on his own?') and say the study was of carers in the last year of the person's life.

scores.accuracy_concern: Carer's leave and day-one flexible working requests apply to employees in England, Scotland and Wales, not Northern Ireland or the self-employed; flexible working is a right to request, which an employer can refuse on set grounds; the Carer's Allowance earnings limit changes each April.
scores.sharpen: Open at the decision point ('Before you give up work to care, check four things') and say plainly that a flexible working request can be refused.

scores.accuracy_concern: Exact NICE NG67 wording on when-required directions needs checking; the CHUMS study was in care homes, not home care, so it should not supply home care error figures; care workers work from the medicines administration record and care plan as well as the label.
scores.sharpen: Quote the NICE NG67 recommendation directly, and check it against any C06 or C16 candidate on medicines in social care before scheduling.

scores.accuracy_concern: The proportion of older people who provide unpaid care needs a verified census figure; NICE NG150 wording on identifying carers should be checked; avoid implying the dependent person is always unsafe.
scores.sharpen: Add one verified figure for the share of people over 65 who provide unpaid care, and schedule apart from its public counterpart C18-22.

scores.accuracy_concern: Benefit rules and rates change each April and Scotland now uses Carer Support Payment; the underlying entitlement only adds money for people who get or could get means-tested benefits; the sources are gov.uk and charity factsheets not opened in this project, which the evidence rules treat as insufficient on their own.
scores.sharpen: Say in the first two lines who this helps (older carers on low incomes who get or could get Pension Credit), give no figures that will date, and send readers to a benefits check.

scores.values_concern: Make sure the reframing does not read as 'caring is good for you' or play down carer strain.
scores.accuracy_concern: The strain estimate's lower bound is 1.00, so it is borderline; lower mortality in population studies probably reflects healthier people taking on care and does not show that caring protects health; a cohort relative risk must not become 'X times more likely' language.
scores.sharpen: End on the practical instruction (ask each carer directly about strain) rather than on the population finding.

scores.values_concern: Describe young carers without pathologising their families or implying a grandchild's help is wrong in itself.
scores.accuracy_concern: The survey was an online convenience sample of 15 to 17 year olds in six countries, so the positive-outcomes finding does not describe all young carers; the Canadian 40% figure should not stand in for the UK; the census count of young carers needs verifying.
scores.sharpen: Drop the European outcome comparison and use one verified UK figure on young carers, keeping the focus on asking and on the right to a young carer's assessment.

scores.values_concern: Make clear that the evidence gap is not an argument for cutting respite services.
scores.accuracy_concern: Check whether the 2014 Cochrane review has been updated; the 2026 review's possible benefits come from studies at high risk of bias or with some concerns, so do not present them as confirmation.
scores.sharpen: Put 'few, poor trials is an evidence gap, not proof that breaks fail' in plain words on the visual and keep the two judging questions as the close.

scores.accuracy_concern: Quote the GMC paragraph exactly, including that the doctor should explain they may not be able to keep the conversation from the patient; nurses and allied professionals follow their own codes; sharing personal information still needs consent or another lawful basis.
scores.sharpen: Add the patient-side action: ask and record who the patient is happy for information to go to, so the next clinician does not repeat the refusal.

scores.accuracy_concern: Care Act section 10(5) wording is 'able, and is likely to continue to be able' and 'willing, and is likely to continue to be willing'; the Scottish section needs confirming; the council must consider willingness, which is not a promise to provide whatever is asked.
scores.sharpen: Add one sentence on what follows (the support plan, and a review of the cared-for person's own care) so carers see that stating a limit leads somewhere.

scores.accuracy_concern: The English duty's section number is uncertain (the Health and Care Act 2022 inserted a discharge duty into the NHS Act 2006); state it only after checking the text; the Scottish duty sits with health boards under the Carers (Scotland) Act 2016.
scores.sharpen: Same core idea as C18-01 for a public audience; run it only if C18-01 is not chosen, or fold its four questions into C18-01's family-facing variant.

scores.values_concern: Use the figure that more than 90% believed the death was a relief to the person with great care or not at all, since it can read as a judgement that life with dementia is not worth living; frame relief as the end of strain and suffering.
scores.accuracy_concern: Single US sample of carers in a trial, in the final year of life; relief was self-reported; mention the minority with prolonged grief only if a verified figure is found.
scores.sharpen: Add one sentence that relief and grief often come together, and name where carers can get support before the death.

scores.accuracy_concern: Effect sizes were small (d 0.23 to 0.30); the DEMQOL difference needs a plain reading; check the 19.7% positive-interactions figure against the paper; antipsychotic use did not fall.
scores.sharpen: Frame around what care staff were given (training, protected time, champions) so it belongs to the workforce category, and check overlap with C08 and C16 care home candidates.

scores.accuracy_concern: Mostly cross-sectional associations; positive aspects may reflect lower strain rather than protect against it; check the wording on self-rated health and personal strain against the review.
scores.sharpen: Consider folding the 'what keeps you going' question into C18-06 or C18-15 rather than running a third carer-assessment question post.

scores.values_concern: Present carer stress as a reason to support carers, never as the 'cause' of a care home move or a failing of the carer.
scores.accuracy_concern: The review searched to 2006; 'wish to place' predicting placement is close to circular; the incontinence finding needs checking against a newer meta-analysis (such as Toot 2017) before it is highlighted; predictors are observational.
scores.sharpen: Check against a newer review and lead with the action (assess the carer's stress directly as part of the plan) rather than the incontinence point.

scores.accuracy_concern: Flu vaccine eligibility wording differs between England and Scotland and is set each season; in England carer eligibility depends on Carer's Allowance or main-carer status; the national programme letters were not opened.
scores.sharpen: Schedule for early autumn only, and add one line on what else being recorded as a carer can lead to, such as a carer's assessment.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Carers (Scotland) Act section on emergency planning and the NICE NG150 wording need checking; name an emergency card scheme only if one is verified.
scores.sharpen: Give the England route as well (ask for a contingency plan in the carer's assessment) so the post works for readers across the UK; schedule apart from C18-09.

scores.values_concern: Leading with 'quality was better when unemployment was higher' can read as welcoming unemployment; keep the point on staff stability and working conditions.
scores.accuracy_concern: Ecological US panel data; Maben 2012 concerned hospital nursing staff, not care workers; the turnover figure is unverified; the chain invites a causal reading that reducing turnover alone improves quality.
scores.sharpen: Replace the unemployment lead with UK evidence on care worker retention and care home quality (for example Allan and Vadean 2021, if verified), or merge the point into C18-05.

scores.values_concern: Avoid stereotyping any group; describe cultural fit in concrete service terms, without reference to religion.
scores.accuracy_concern: Review of 13 studies with few direct comparisons between groups; do not claim how often services use the phrase; present it as a quoted belief.
scores.sharpen: Give practitioners one concrete check to run in their own service, such as whether carer assessments are offered with a professional interpreter.

scores.accuracy_concern: The key 2026 review abstract was only partly read; the claim that carers report problems patients do not needs a source; the patient's agreement to involve the carer should be mentioned.
scores.sharpen: Read the review results and merge with C18-08 or a C06 medicines post if one already covers the carer's role in medication review.

scores.accuracy_concern: Regulation 9A applies in England only, to CQC-registered providers, and says people should not be discouraged from being accompanied, with exceptions; the Scottish position (Anne's Law) is uncertain and should be left out unless verified; the regulation text was not opened.
scores.sharpen: Quote the regulation's own wording from the CQC guidance and say it applies in England, since many of the account's readers are in Scotland.

scores.accuracy_concern: Best-interests law applies only when the person lacks capacity for the decision about where to live; if they have capacity the choice is theirs, but it cannot oblige a carer to provide care; the post should state this distinction.
scores.sharpen: Add the capacity distinction in one sentence and replace 'Both of those facts deserve a hearing' with a concrete opening situation.

allocation_reason: 26 of 27 candidates score 36 or more with no disqualifying flag, the earlier collection had almost nothing on carers or the care workforce, and the top 14 are distinct across audiences and series, with strong reserves (C18-05, C18-06, C18-10) if any legislation-based post fails verification.
balance_note: Top 14: 6 practitioners (14, 11, 01, 09, 08, 12), 5 public (15, 22, 17, 02, 07), 3 both (13, 04, 03); series spread across Teaching round, Ask this, Reading the evidence, Care that works, What gets counted, Who gets left out, Weighing it up and Small detail. Most explain or teach rather than criticise. The paid care workforce is thin (only 03 and 08); C18-05 (count the different care workers) is the best workforce reserve and should replace 12 or 08 if workforce coverage is wanted. About half of the top 14 (14, 15, 22, 02, 07, 09, 08) rest on legislation, GMC or NICE text not yet opened, so verify early. Schedule pairs apart: 01 and 16, 09 and 22, 06 and 17 (same Schulz 2003 source), 02, 15 and 27 (carer's assessment).
